```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(formex)
```

When `guess_data_type()` looks at a column, part of the work is done by
detectors (see *How Detectors Recognize a Type*). But the first stage --- the
**router** that proposes which types are even worth checking --- is a trained
model, and a model cannot read raw strings. It needs numbers. So before anything
is guessed, the column is turned into a fixed list of numbers that *summarize*
it: its **feature profile**. Building that profile is called **feature
engineering**, and this guide explains what goes into it and what it can and
cannot capture.

## The idea: describe a column with numbers

Think about how *you* tell an ID column from a name column at a glance. You
don't read every value --- you notice things: the ID values are all the same
length, all digits, every one different; the names are words, start with a
capital, repeat, and many are ones you recognize. Feature engineering writes
down those impressions as numbers.

`fx_extract_features()` does this. Give it a column and it returns one row of
summary numbers:

```{r extract}
f <- fx_extract_features(c("James", "Mary", "Robert", "Linda", "James"))
dim(f)       # one row of features for the whole column
f[c("n", "n_unique", "unique_ratio", "len_mean", "pct_chr_alpha", "lex_first_name_token")]
```

Read that row as the model would: five values, four distinct, all letters, and
--- the giveaway --- every one is a known first name (`lex_first_name_token` is
`1`). That last number alone almost settles it.

Every column, whatever its contents, is reduced to the **same** fixed set of
numbers, so the router can compare any column against the patterns it learned
during training.

## What goes into the profile

The numbers are organized into **blocks**, each capturing a different kind of
signal. Here is the live inventory from the installed package:

```{r blocks}
man <- fx_feature_manifest()
as.data.frame(table(block = man$block), responseName = "n_features")
```

```{r blocks-hidden, echo = FALSE}
total <- nrow(man)
```

That is `r total` numbers in all. What each block is looking at, in plain terms:

- **core** --- the column's shape as a whole: how many values, how many are
  missing, how many are *distinct*, whether every value is unique (a strong hint
  for an ID), whether one value dominates. This is the "is it a key? a constant?
  a handful of repeated categories?" signal.
- **length** --- how long the values are, and how much the length *varies*. IDs
  and codes are often all one length; names and addresses vary a lot.
- **charclass** --- the mix of character kinds: what share are letters, digits,
  punctuation, whitespace, uppercase.
- **charfreq** --- the frequencies of individual letters and digits, including
  the **first** and **last** character distributions. This is surprisingly
  powerful: the last letter of a word carries morphology (names ending in
  *-a*, *-n*), and leading characters separate, say, `B0`-prefixed product codes
  from ordinary text.
- **punct** --- where and how often punctuation appears (and how regularly). A
  phone number, a date, and an IP address each have a signature arrangement of
  separators.
- **token** --- structure when values are split into words/pieces: how many
  tokens, and whether the first and last token are stable across the column
  (the word-level version of fixed punctuation).
- **mask** --- how well the values fit fixed positional shapes (the
  digit/letter templates the `mask` detectors use).
- **regex** --- hit rates against a battery of pattern probes.
- **numeric** --- when values are numbers: their range, whether they are whole,
  signed, bounded 0--1, their spread and skew. This is the block the `shape`
  types lean on.
- **sequence** --- run-length and ordering signals (e.g. values that look like a
  sequential counter).
- **lexicon** --- the share of values that appear in built-in reference lists:
  common first names, surnames, US cities, countries, states. These
  membership rates are among the **strongest** signals the router has for
  telling the easily-confused people/place columns apart.
- **header** --- features of the column's *name*, when one is supplied, for the
  cases where the values are silent.

Blocks are computed independently, so the engine can skip ones a given model
does not use. Missing or not-applicable numbers are recorded as `NA`, never as
zero, so "no digits here" is never confused with "a digit value of zero."

## From profile to shortlist

The feature profile feeds the **router**, which proposes a short list of likely
types. Two routers ship:

- a **learned** model (gradient-boosted trees) trained on thousands of labeled
  columns' profiles --- the default when it is installed;
- a **signature** router that needs no model: it reduces the profile to a short
  numeric fingerprint and ranks ontology types by how close their known examples
  sit to the column.

Either way the profile is the input. The verifier stage then confirms the
shortlist's candidates with their actual recipes (see *Guessing a Column's
Type*), so a feature-based shortlist never gets the final word by itself.

## Where it works well --- and where it struggles

The honest summary: **the model is only as good as the signal the values
carry.** Where a type leaves a fingerprint in how its values are written,
feature-based guessing is excellent. Where two types look identical as values,
no amount of feature engineering can separate them.

**Works well** (the structure is in the values):

- **Dates and times** --- the parse either succeeds or it doesn't; recognition
  is near-perfect.
- **Names and geographies** --- the lexicon-membership features are decisive:
  a column of values that are mostly known first names is almost unmistakable.
- **Shaped identifiers** --- EINs, ISBNs, UUIDs, hashes: fixed length, fixed
  alphabet, often a checksum.

**Struggles** (the signal is not in the values):

- **Numeric subtypes.** A *count*, a *score*, an *index*, and a *rate* are all
  just numbers. The `numeric` block can say "this is a bounded whole number,"
  but it cannot say *which* kind of quantity it is --- that needs the column
  name or a codebook. The router sensibly keeps these columns shallow rather
  than guessing a leaf.
- **Surrogate / record keys.** A membership ID is a column of unique integers,
  which looks like any other column of unique integers. The `core` block flags
  "this is probably a key," but it cannot say *what entity* it keys.
- **Free text.** Notes and descriptions have no recognizable form.
- **Unfamiliar data.** On data unlike anything the model trained on, it is far
  better at the broad call ("this is a number / a date / a code") than at the
  exact leaf. Measured on an outside corpus during development, the model's
  confidence in the broad `data_type` held around **0.70** while its confidence
  in the exact leaf fell to about **0.48** --- which is exactly why
  `guess_data_type()` reports a path *prefix* and stops early rather than forcing
  a precise but unreliable leaf.

As a development benchmark (3-fold out-of-fold on roughly 3,850 labeled columns,
measured during model fitting and not recomputed here), the learned router
placed the correct type in its top choice about **77%** of the time and in its
top five about **94%** --- with the easy families (dates, names) near-perfect and
the value-undetectable ones (numeric subtypes, record keys) carrying the misses.
The strongest single feature, by a wide margin, was the first-name
lexicon-membership rate --- a reminder that a good reference list often beats a
clever statistic.
